item.title: Administrative Inequality: Conceptualization and Micro-Mechanisms
item.content:encoded:
Steffen Eckhard, Leibniz University Hannover

Eva Thomann, University of Konstanz

Gabriela Lotta, Fundação Getulio Vargas

Sharon Gilad, Hebrew University of Jerusalem

Public administrations worldwide generate social and political inequality through organizational practices and administrative decisions. Research on this phenomenon is fragmented across multiple subfields with different terminology, preventing coherent understanding. This special issue proposes 'administrative inequality' as a unifying concept to integrate these perspectives.

Administrative inequality is defined as any administrative rule, process, or behavior that systematically impedes citizens' equal opportunity to access public services they legally claim. Grounded in equal opportunity theory, this definition examines how micro-level behaviors and organizational conditions jointly produce unequal access, acknowledging context-dependent variations across different institutional settings.

item.title: Coping with tensions, challenges and limitations of boundary spanning work in collaborative governance and public service delivery in turbulent times
item.content:encoded:
Ingmar van Meerkerk, Erasmus University Rotterdam

Anka Kekez, University of Zagreb

Jurian Edelenbos, Erasmus University Rotterdam

This special issue addresses how boundary spanners navigate tensions and challenges while fostering cross-boundary collaboration and public service delivery in turbulent governance environments. It seeks to advance research on collaborative governance by examining the practices, role tensions, and coping strategies of individuals who work across organizational, sectoral, and community boundaries to address complex societal challenges such as sustainability transitions and social inequality. The issue recognizes that these boundary spanning workers operate under increasingly difficult conditions marked by fragmentation, institutional discontinuities, and competing logics.

item.title: Place-Based Strategy Design for Value Creation
item.content:encoded:
Carmine Bianchi, University of Palermo

Greta Nasi, Bocconi University

Bin Chen, Baruch College

Gabriela Lotta, FGV-São Paulo School of Business Administration

Public administrations confront increasingly multifaceted challenges such as social inequality, climate change, and digital transformation that standard management approaches struggle to address. The call invites examination of how place-based strategy design can foster sustainable value creation by integrating organizational capabilities with local ecosystemic contexts, moving beyond traditional linear and centralized planning models toward adaptive, collaborative approaches grounded in specific spatial, cultural, and institutional conditions.

The special issue seeks contributions that advance understanding of how public value emerges from interactions between internal strategic intent and external community demands, mediated by place-specific factors termed locus and habitus. It emphasizes the need for performance management systems sensitive to local diversity, collaborative governance platforms, and methods that balance inside-out organizational perspectives with outside-in ecosystem thinking to address wicked problems effectively.
